1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
5	The central finding of our experiments is that restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
6	ESS-only reweighting---which maximizes $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$---degrades PPL to 17.723, \emph{worse} than the uniform baseline (17.694, Table~\ref{tab:main}).
7	The dual-constrained adaptive $\bstar$, by contrast, achieves 17.651 by selecting the \emph{smallest} $b$ that meets the quality floor $\tau$.
8	The mechanism is clear from the binding statistics: in the 40.1\% of reweighted batches where $\aeff$ binds, mean $\bstar = 1.67$ versus 4.15 under ESS-only---a 2.5$\times$ less aggressive exponent that retains ESS\,=\,2.60, well above the floor $\nmin = 2$.
9	Over-downweighting discards gradient signal from borderline samples whose detector scores are intermediate (e.g., $q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$); these samples carry partial but non-negligible training value, and aggressively suppressing them impoverishes the effective training distribution.
10	The $\aeff$ constraint prevents this by halting $b$ as soon as the quality target is met.
11	
12	\paragraph{$\tau$ as a practical dial.}
13	The quality threshold $\tau$ controls the trade-off between decontamination strength and sample retention.
14	Our sweep (Table~\ref{tab:tau}) reveals a wide safe operating range: all $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ outperform uniform training, with PPL varying only 0.035 across this interval.
15	The sensitivity is asymmetric---under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) incurs mild degradation ($-$0.006 to $-$0.015 vs.\ uniform), while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bar{b}^* = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$, 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$).
16	This asymmetry reinforces the minimum intervention intuition: the cost of doing too little is small, whereas the cost of doing too much is steep.
17	We recommend $\tau = 0.8$ as a principled default; practitioners operating at different contamination rates can adjust within the safe range with low risk.
18	
19	\paragraph{Connection to convergence theory.}
20	\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} prove that pretraining convergence rate scales with $\alpha$, the effective real data fraction.
21	Our $\tau$ serves an analogous role---setting a floor on the weighted real proportion per batch---but an important distinction must be noted: their analysis assumes a known contamination proportion, whereas our method estimates quality from detector scores without access to the true $\alpha$.
22	We therefore position $\tau$ as an empirical hyperparameter with theoretical motivation: convergence theory explains \emph{why} a quality threshold improves training, while the specific value of $\tau$ is determined empirically.
23	Bridging this gap---deriving $\tau$ from first principles without known proportions---is an open theoretical question.
24	
25	\section*{Limitations}
26	\label{sec:limitations}
27	
28	\paragraph{Scale.}
29	All experiments use a single model size (Qwen3-0.6B) with batch size 4.
30	Batch-level $q$-score statistics concentrate differently at larger batch sizes typical of 3B+ training; the optimal $\tau$ range and constraint dynamics may shift at scale.
31	
32	\paragraph{Contamination distribution.}
33	We inject synthetic data via uniform random mixing at a controlled ratio ($\rho{=}0.4$).
34	Real web-scale contamination is domain-skewed, which may alter within-batch $\aeff$ distributions and require domain-aware extensions.
35	
36	\paragraph{Detector coverage.}
37	We evaluate one detector family (TF-IDF + logistic regression).
38	Although our results suggest calibration dominates discrimination for reweighting quality, a systematic ablation across detector architectures and quality levels is needed.
39	
40	\paragraph{Threshold.}
41	$\tau$ is an empirical hyperparameter.
42	The convergence theory of \citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} assumes a known contamination proportion $\alpha$, which we do not require; bridging this gap to derive $\tau$ from first principles remains open.
43	
44	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
45	We report held-out perplexity only.
46	Downstream task evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag) would strengthen the practical case, particularly at scales where PPL differences translate more reliably to task performance.
47	
48	\paragraph{Effect size.}
49	The PPL improvement over uniform weighting is 0.041 at 0.6B/40\% contamination ($\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}} = -0.041$ at $\tau{=}0.8$).
50	While consistent across seeds, this effect is modest; we expect amplification at higher contamination ratios and larger model scales, but verification is ongoing.
51	
52	\paragraph{Batch size sensitivity.}
53	At batch size 8 with $\nmin = 2$, the ESS floor becomes a weak constraint ($\nmin / B = 0.25$), and performance degrades (PPL\,=\,17.73).
54	The coupling $\nmin \approx \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ should be validated as batch size scales; a relative threshold ($\nmin = \gamma B$ for some $\gamma$) may generalize better than a fixed integer.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

% Claim 1: Dual > ESS-only (3 seeds)
ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
The degradation is consistent: ESS-only exceeds uniform on every individual seed (Table~\ref{tab:main}), ruling out seed-specific artifacts.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to systematic over-downweighting, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.
Conversely, adaptive (dual) improves over uniform on all three seeds (by 0.041, 0.043, and 0.045 respectively), confirming that the $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ quality floor prevents the over-intervention that plagues ESS-only.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Seed 42} & \textbf{Seed 123} & \textbf{Seed 456} & \textbf{Mean} \\
\midrule
Uniform               & 17.694 & 17.686 & 17.702 & 17.694 \\
Grid-best ($b{=}0.5$) & \textbf{17.651} & \textbf{17.638} & \textbf{17.650} & \textbf{17.646} \\
ESS-only               & 17.730 & 17.720 & 17.719 & 17.723 \\
Golden Ratio$^\dagger$ & 17.654 & --     & --     & --     \\
\midrule
Adaptive (ours)        & 17.653 & 17.643 & 17.657 & 17.651 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Held-out perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$).
Grid-best selects the optimal fixed $b$ post-hoc from six candidates.
$^\dagger$Evaluated on seed 42 only.
Best per column in \textbf{bold}.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

\subsection{Sensitivity Analysis}

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
Table~\ref{tab:tau} varies $\tau$ while holding $n_{\min} = 2$ (seed 42).
All values in $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ improve over uniform, with $\tau = 0.8$ achieving the lowest PPL (17.653).
Higher $\tau$ demands greater $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$, forcing the solver to increase $b^*$: mean $\bar{b}^*$ rises monotonically from 0.39 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$.
Below 0.8, reweighting is too gentle to fully exploit the detector signal; above, $b^*$ inflates past diminishing returns and PPL degrades.
The range $[0.5, 0.8]$ provides a wide safe operating region, with $\tau = 0.8$ as the recommended default.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}cccc@{}}
\toprule
$\tau$ & \textbf{PPL} & $\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}}$ & $\bar{b}^*$ \\
\midrule
0.50 & 17.688 & $-$0.006 & 0.39 \\
0.60 & 17.681 & $-$0.013 & 0.59 \\
0.70 & 17.679 & $-$0.015 & 0.89 \\
\textbf{0.80} & \textbf{17.653} & $\mathbf{-0.041}$ & \textbf{1.40} \\
0.90 & 17.712 & $+$0.018 & 2.36 \\
0.95 & 17.723 & $+$0.029 & 3.08 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Sensitivity to $\tau$ (seed 42, $n_{\min}{=}2$, $\rho{=}0.4$).
$\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}}$: PPL change vs.\ uniform baseline (17.694).
$\bar{b}^*$: mean adaptive exponent across batches.}
\label{tab:tau}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Minimum ESS $n_{\min}$.}
Table~\ref{tab:nmin} ablates $n_{\min}$ at batch size $B{=}4$.
Removing the ESS floor ($n_{\min} = 1$) allows $b^*$ to inflate to mean 7.20, degrading PPL to 17.789---0.095 worse than uniform.
At $n_{\min} = 2$ ($= \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$), $b^*$ is constrained to mean 1.40 and PPL reaches 17.653, verified across three seeds.
At $n_{\min} = B = 4$, the ESS constraint is trivially satisfied at $b^* = 0$ for every batch, and PPL reverts to the uniform level (17.695 vs.\ 17.694).
The results exhibit a U-shaped pattern: too-low $n_{\min}$ permits over-downweighting, while $n_{\min}$ at or near $B$ removes the ability to reweight.

The coupling between $n_{\min}$ and $B$ extends beyond the $B{=}4$ setting.
At batch size $B{=}8$ with $n_{\min}{=}2$, the ESS range $[2, 8]$ is wide enough that the stability constraint rarely binds, yielding PPL 17.73---comparable to ESS-only and 0.036 worse than uniform.
This confirms that $n_{\min}$ must scale with $B$: a fixed $n_{\min}$ that works for one batch size can degrade to near-ESS-only behavior at larger $B$.
The rule $n_{\min} = \max(2, \lfloor B/2 \rfloor)$ keeps the ESS constraint active without over-restricting the solver, and we recommend it as a practical default.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccc@{}}
\toprule
$n_{\min}$ & \textbf{PPL} & $\bar{b}^*$ \\
\midrule

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Sensitivity to $n_{\min}$ (seed 42, $B{=}4$, $\tau{=}0.8$).
$n_{\min} = 4 = B$ forces $b^* = 0$ on all batches, recovering uniform weighting.
$^\ddagger$From an earlier adaptive configuration; not an independent ablation.}
\label{tab:nmin}
\end{table}

\subsection{Main Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity across methods and seeds.
Adaptive reweighting achieves mean PPL 17.651, matching grid-best ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance: the per-seed gap never exceeds 0.007, less than half the cross-seed range of the uniform baseline (17.686--17.702).
This parity comes at zero validation cost---grid search requires $|\mathcal{B}|$ complete training runs (six in our sweep), whereas adaptive requires one.

The grid-$b$ sweep reveals monotonically increasing PPL from $b{=}0.5$ to $b{=}5.0$ (17.651 to 17.818 on seed 42; full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:grid}), confirming that exponent selection is consequential.
The optimal $b{=}0.5$ differs from the $b{=}10$ reported by \citet{drayson2025detection} at comparable model scale, underscoring the model-dependence of fixed-exponent selection.

ESS-only (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.723 across three seeds, \emph{worse} than uniform (17.694) by 0.029.
Removing $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and maximizing $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$ leads to over-downweighting that degrades training, providing direct evidence for the minimum-intervention principle.

The Golden Ratio oracle~\citep{he2025golden} achieves PPL 17.654 on seed 42 using known provenance labels.
Adaptive reaches within 0.001 of this upper bound without provenance access, suggesting the dual constraint recovers near-optimal weights from noisy detector scores alone.

The adaptive $b^*$ distribution (median 0.87, IQR $[0.54, 1.51]$, mean 1.40) confirms that most batches need only moderate intervention.
The constraint regime breakdown in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} shows that $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ prevents over-intervention in the 40\% of reweighted batches where moderate $b$ already meets the quality target.

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
5	The central finding of our experiments is that restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
6	ESS-only reweighting---which maximizes $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$---degrades PPL to 17.723, \emph{worse} than the uniform baseline (17.694, Table~\ref{tab:main}).
7	The dual-constrained adaptive $\bstar$, by contrast, achieves 17.651 by selecting the \emph{smallest} $b$ that meets the quality floor $\tau$.
8	The mechanism is clear from the binding statistics: in the 40.1\% of reweighted batches where $\aeff$ binds, mean $\bstar = 1.67$ versus 4.15 under ESS-only---a 2.5$\times$ less aggressive exponent that retains ESS\,=\,2.60, well above the floor $\nmin = 2$.
9	Over-downweighting discards gradient signal from borderline samples whose detector scores are intermediate (e.g., $q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$); these samples carry partial but non-negligible training value, and aggressively suppressing them impoverishes the effective training distribution.
10	The $\aeff$ constraint prevents this by halting $b$ as soon as the quality target is met.
11	
12	\paragraph{$\tau$ as a practical dial.}
13	The quality threshold $\tau$ controls the trade-off between decontamination strength and sample retention.
14	Our sweep (Table~\ref{tab:tau}) reveals a wide safe operating range: all $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ outperform uniform training, with PPL varying only 0.035 across this interval.
15	The sensitivity is asymmetric---under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) incurs mild degradation ($-$0.006 to $-$0.015 vs.\ uniform), while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bar{b}^* = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$, 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$).
16	This asymmetry reinforces the minimum intervention intuition: the cost of doing too little is small, whereas the cost of doing too much is steep.
17	We recommend $\tau = 0.8$ as a principled default; practitioners operating at different contamination rates can adjust within the safe range with low risk.
18	
19	\paragraph{Connection to convergence theory.}
20	\citet{wang2026survive} prove that pretraining convergence rate scales with $\alpha$, the effective real data fraction.
21	Our $\tau$ serves an analogous role---setting a floor on the weighted real proportion per batch---but an important distinction must be noted: their analysis assumes a known contamination proportion, whereas our method estimates quality from detector scores without access to the true $\alpha$.
22	We therefore position $\tau$ as an empirical hyperparameter with theoretical motivation: convergence theory explains \emph{why} a quality threshold improves training, while the specific value of $\tau$ is determined empirically.
23	Bridging this gap---deriving $\tau$ from first principles without known proportions---is an open theoretical question.
24	
25	\section*{Limitations}
26	\label{sec:limitations}
27	
28	\paragraph{Scale.}
29	All experiments use a single model size (Qwen3-0.6B) with batch size 4.
30	Batch-level $q$-score statistics concentrate differently at larger batch sizes typical of 3B+ training; the optimal $\tau$ range and constraint dynamics may shift at scale.
31	
32	\paragraph{Contamination distribution.}
33	We inject synthetic data via uniform random mixing at a controlled ratio ($\rho{=}0.4$).
34	Real web-scale contamination is domain-skewed, which may alter within-batch $\aeff$ distributions and require domain-aware extensions.
35	
36	\paragraph{Detector coverage.}
37	We evaluate one detector family (TF-IDF + logistic regression).
38	Although our results suggest calibration dominates discrimination for reweighting quality, a systematic ablation across detector architectures and quality levels is needed.
39	
40	\paragraph{Threshold.}
41	The binary threshold in the detection step introduces a hard boundary between synthetic and human-authored text; see Section~\ref{sec:discussion} for discussion of theoretical connections and potential continuous relaxations.
42	
43	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
44	We report held-out perplexity only.
45	Downstream task evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag) would strengthen the practical case, particularly at scales where PPL differences translate more reliably to task performance.
46	
47	\paragraph{Effect size.}
48	The PPL improvement over uniform weighting is 0.041 at 0.6B/40\% contamination ($\Delta_{\mathrm{unif}} = -0.041$ at $\tau{=}0.8$).
49	While consistent across seeds, this effect is modest; we expect amplification at higher contamination ratios and larger model scales, but verification is ongoing.
50	
51	\paragraph{Batch size sensitivity.}
52	At batch size 8 with $\nmin = 2$, the ESS floor becomes a weak constraint ($\nmin / B = 0.25$), and performance degrades (PPL\,=\,17.73).
53	The coupling $\nmin \approx \lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ should be validated as batch size scales; a relative threshold ($\nmin = \gamma B$ for some $\gamma$) may generalize better than a fixed integer.

Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng2025contamination}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov2024model} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson2025detection} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he2025golden} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng2025beyond} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.

On Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining with 40\% synthetic contamination (132M+ tokens from FineWeb), adaptive reweighting achieves mean held-out perplexity of 17.651 across three seeds, matching the grid-searched optimum ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance (\S\ref{sec:results}).

The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson2025detection} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he2025golden} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng2025beyond} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang2026survive}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.
